title: Adab of guests
hookLine: strangers at Abraham's door, a lamp put out in Medina, and a hadith with two sides

lines: A FATTED CALF, SET BEFORE THEM.
cards: Strangers arrive at Abraham's door. They greet him with peace, and he answers with peace. He doesn't know them, and the Qur'an says he noted that to himself.
Then, without asking who they are, he slips away to his household and comes back with a fatted calf, sets it in front of them, and asks why they aren't eating.

Surah al-Dhariyat opens the scene, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee (O Muhammad)?" You met them on day thirty-eight. Today's adab starts at that door.

teach.h: WHOEVER BELIEVES, LET HIM HONOR HIS GUEST.
teach.b: The hadith opens the way the speech hadith did. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.
Faith, showing up at the door. Another report in Bukhari spells it out: the guest's special due is a day and a night.

teach.h: A DAY AND A NIGHT; THREE DAYS.
teach.b: Hospitality is three days. Anything beyond that is charity. And it isn't right for a guest to stay until he becomes a burden.

teach.h: THE GUEST DOESN'T BURDEN THE HOST.
teach.b: The host honors; the guest doesn't weigh on the host. Adab runs both ways at the door. Then a story, also in Bukhari, of how far honoring can go.
A hungry man came to the Prophet, and his households had nothing but water.

teach.h: THE LAMP PUT OUT IN MEDINA.
teach.b: A man of the Ansar, the people of Medina, took the guest home. His wife said there was only enough for the children. So they settled the children to sleep, set out the food, and put out the lamp.
In the dark they moved their hands as if eating, so their guest could eat his fill and never know. In the morning the Prophet told the man that Allah was pleased with what the two of them had done.
The hadith says a verse of al-Hashr came down about them: people who prefer others above themselves, even when they are in need.

how: Muslims treat hospitality as part of faith, citing the hadith "let him honor his guest" and the story of Abraham's guests, and teach guests in turn not to overstay or burden their hosts.

o: serving guests the most expensive food you can
letting any guest stay as long as they like
honoring a guest, and a guest not burdening the host

games.q: the adab of guests — tap the pairs.
p: set a fatted calf before strangers
put out the lamp so the guest could eat

s: in the hadith, a guest may stay as long as he likes
hospitality is three days, beyond that it's charity, and a guest shouldn't stay until he burdens the host.
Abraham questioned his guests before feeding them
they were unknown to him, and the verses record no question before he brought the food.
the guest hadith opens like the speech hadith
both begin: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day.

games.q: a hungry guest comes home with you. your wife says there's only enough for the children's supper. what do you do?
o: send the guest on to someone else.
settle the children, put out the lamp, and let the guest eat.
split it so everyone gets a little.
games.why: in Bukhari, an Ansari couple ate nothing in the dark so their guest could eat his fill. the hadith says a verse of al-Hashr came down about them.

practice: Bring to mind one person you could host, at a table, over tea, or simply by making room for them in a busy day, and see them arriving at your door.

What would you set in front of them, not the fanciest thing but the warmest, and how would you make sure they leave light, never feeling like a burden? If you pray, you can make du'a for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Adab of guests. The manners of the door: the host honors the guest, and the guest takes care not to burden the host. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: guest, the word in the hadith and in the story of Abraham's guests.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the guest. A good guest doesn't weigh on the host. See you tomorrow, on the road.

sources.q: Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee (O Muhammad)?

sources.ref: Qur'an 51:25–27 (peace, folk unknown, a fatted calf, will ye not eat)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, 6135 (let him honor his guest; a day and a night; three days; beyond that is charity; not to stay until he burdens him)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3798 (the Ansari couple and the lamp)
Qur'an 59:9 (they prefer others above themselves, though in need)
